title: King's Physicist wins Turing AI Fellowship to revolutionise neutrino detection and nuclear safety
excerpt: The approach could offer a clearer image of neutrino and fundamental particle activity than state-of-the-art detectors.
content:
The approach could offer a clearer image of neutrino and fundamental particle activity than state-of-the-art detectors.

Dr Thiago Sogo Bezerra, Lecturer in Physics, has been named as a Turing AI Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellow.

One of twenty new fellows supported by £39 million in government funding to build the UK’s AI capacity and solve some of society’s biggest challenges, Dr Bezerra hopes to use artificial intelligence to fundamentally change how we measure neutrinos and monitor nuclear safety.

Neutrinos, the particles at the centre of this year’s Nobel Prize in Physics, are among the most common in the universe, yet interact so weakly that trillions pass through the human body every second without leaving a trace. They are created in nuclear reactions and other high-energy processes. Radioactive potassium in our bodies gives off 4,000 a second, the nuclear fusion that powers the sun releases 2 x 1038 a second, and exploding stars and other violent events far beyond our solar system send them across the cosmos. 

Trillions of them hit almost every surface of the earth every second, but learning about them is difficult as neutrinos interact with other particles so rarely. Using specialised experiments like Hyper-Kamiokande designed to catch these rare interactions, scientists hope to investigate the nature of cosmic phenomena. 

While there are many types of neutrino detectors, typically they are incredibly large, filled with transparent liquids like pure water and shielded from outside radiation that may interfere with their highly sensitive photosensors. This gives them the best chance of catching the rare moments when a neutrino strikes an atom. While allowing for these photosensors to pick up on the bursts of light that occur when neutrinos and the contents of the experiment’s tank interact, this poses several logistical and cost challenges. Hyper-Kamiokande is 260,000-ton pure water tank miles below the earth’s surface and uses 40,000 expensive, high-end photosensors.

When uranium or plutonium atoms split apart in a reactor, the unstable fragments they leave behind release neutrinos as they decay. Close to a reactor, these neutrinos stream out in far greater numbers than from natural sources, giving detectors a much stronger signal. By using a reactor as an intense, steady source of neutrinos, Dr Bezerra’s LiquidO paves the way for much smaller and cheaper detectors.

Furthermore, by using a novel opaque medium instead of a clear one, LiquidO offers a clearer image of neutrino and fundamental particle activity than state-of-the-art detectors.

Threading optical fibres through a two-metre diameter and four-metre-long cylinder of opaque scintillator material, LiquidO accurately captures the topology of individual fundamental particles as they interact with the detector. The target material confines the light which comes from interaction between the medium and neutrino, making it easier to identify individual interactions which happen close to one another. Using AI that Dr Bezerra hopes to refine further during the fellowship, the detector paints a picture of the interactions and their strength while filtering out noise to more effectively than current methods.

Because the target is already opaque, the team behind LiquidO also hope that it can serve as a test bed for ‘doping’ scintillator with elements like indium or copper, that may have novel interactions with fundamental particles. As the approach allows picks up low-energy neutrinos more effectively than other detectors, the researchers hope it may be used to study geoneutrinos which result from the extreme heat and pressure at the earth’s core.

By deeply integrating AI into experimental science, we can further the interdisciplinary impact of the technology to uncover some of physics’ biggest questions – it’s a very exciting time.”

Dr Thiago Sogo Bezerra

The team also believes their technology could be used to efficiently and non-invasively monitor nuclear reactors without the need for costly underground infrastructure. Neutrino emission directly correlates with a reactor’s thermal power and fuel composition, with the proposed system capable of delivering measurements completely independent of reactor operators and even able to pick up on nuclear materials that have been improperly decommissioned.

Commenting on the social and scientific benefits of the fellowship, Dr Bezerra said “Our novel approaches for nuclear detection avoid the need to place costly instruments at the heart of a nuclear power station that could easily be destroyed and rely on the transparency of individual safety officers. We can align directly with international nuclear safeguards and offer an independent method for monitoring reactor operations to shape energy policy and oversight.

“By deeply integrating AI into experimental science, we can also further the interdisciplinary impact of the technology to uncover some of physics’ biggest questions – it’s a very exciting time.”

These fellowships will give outstanding researchers the freedom and support to push the boundaries of AI itself, while also applying it in new ways across a wide range of disciplines.”

Professor Charlotte Deane, Senior Responsible Owner for the UKRI IS8 AI Programme and Executive Chair of EPSRC

Professor Charlotte Deane, Senior Responsible Owner for the UKRI IS8 AI Programme and Executive Chair of EPSRC, said “AI has enormous potential to transform the way we understand and tackle some of the biggest challenges facing society. These fellowships will give outstanding researchers the freedom and support to push the boundaries of AI itself, while also applying it in new ways across a wide range of disciplines.”

The Turing AI Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowships began last month and will run for three years.
